dedupe_keys.name: heat stress mitigation by trees and shelters at bus stops in houston wbgt measurements 2023

description: This study by Kevin Lanza, Sara Ernst, Katie Watkins and Baojiang Chen, published in Transportation Research Part D in 2025, measures how trees and different bus shelter designs affect heat stress at transit stops. Coverage: over 13 summer days in 2023, sensors measured wet bulb globe temperature (WBGT) in tree shade and under four shelter designs, compared with unshaded areas, at 17 bus stops in Houston, Texas, analysed with multilevel linear mixed effects models. Tree-shaded areas were 3.2 C (5.8 F) cooler than unshaded areas; shelters gave less cooling than trees and enclosed shelters less than open designs, and heat stress under unshaded, enclosed shelters was more than 3 C higher than in unshaded areas outside shelters. The authors suggest that tree planting may be a top option for heat safety and that poorly designed shelters may be a form of maladaptation. Format and access: an open article; the TRID record carries the abstract. Licence and cost: free to read. Caveats: 17 stops over 13 days in one city. The measured cooling by shade type can set exposure reductions for waiting passengers in extreme heat climate adaptation models. It relates to the Austin bus stop shade and ridership study and the USGS urban tree canopy data in the catalogue.
